modules.title: Transformer Architectures
modules.summary: Self-attention, the transformer block, and the architectural family tree — the established core beneath the fast-moving frontier of model design. As of October 2026.
objectives: Explain scaled dot-product attention
Describe the transformer block's components
Name the major architectural variants and their motivations
Distinguish settled core from open research questions

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: **Scaled dot-product attention**: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵛ/√d_k)V. Queries match keys; the scores weight the values. **Multi-head** attention runs several of these in parallel subspaces and concatenates. Cost is **quadratic in sequence length** — the fundamental scaling pressure behind every efficiency variant. (Vaswani et al., 'Attention Is All You Need,' 2017.)

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: A transformer block: multi-head attention + position-wise feed-forward network, each wrapped in a **residual connection** and **normalization** (LayerNorm; many modern models use RMSNorm). **Positional information** is injected — originally sinusoidal encodings, now typically **rotary embeddings (RoPE)**. Stack N blocks: that is the model.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Settled patterns: **decoder-only** autoregressive models dominate language modeling; **mixture-of-experts** (sparse expert routing) trades total parameters for active compute; **KV-cache** and its compressions serve long contexts. Active frontier: attention alternatives (state-space models, linear attention), ever-longer effective context, and inference-time compute scaling. Treat any specific 'best' claim as perishable.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: The *mechanism* (attention, residuals, normalization) is settled textbook material. Everything about *which variant wins*, scale records, and benchmark leadership changes in months — verify against current sources before citing. This module teaches the durable core; the daily pipeline appends the moving edge.

cards.back: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵛ/√d_k)V.
The QKᵛ score matrix is n×n in sequence length — the core scaling pressure.
Multi-head attention + feed-forward network, each with residual connection and normalization.
Rotary Position Embedding — the now-standard way to inject positional information.
Sparse routing: many total parameters, few active per token — capacity without proportional compute.

During autoregressive generation, each step would recompute attention over all past tokens; the KV cache stores past keys and values so each new token costs O(n) instead of O(n²) per step. It is the standard inference optimization — memory traded for speed — and the reason long contexts are memory-hungry. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Pre-training vs. post-training in one pass.
cards.back: Pre-training: next-token prediction over trillions of tokens — builds the base model. Post-training: supervised fine-tuning, RLHF/RLAIF, and instruction tuning — shapes the base model into an assistant. Capabilities come mostly from pre-training; behavior and reliability come mostly from post-training. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Why did the transformer displace RNNs and LSTMs?
cards.back: Attention processes all positions in parallel (RNNs are sequential), captures long-range dependencies directly, and scales cleanly with data and compute — the three properties the scaling era needed. Training parallelism, not just quality, decided the architecture war. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The √d_k scaling in attention exists to:
choices: Keep dot products from growing large and saturating softmax
quiz.explain: Large dot products push softmax into flat regions with vanishing gradients; scaling counters it.

quiz.q: A decoder-only model generates text by:
choices: Autoregressive next-token prediction with causal masking
quiz.explain: Causal masking prevents attending to future tokens; generation proceeds left to right.

quiz.q: Residual connections primarily solve:
quiz.explain: Identity shortcuts let gradients flow through dozens of blocks.

quiz.q: Which claim about model architectures is safest long-term?
choices: Model X is the best open model
Attention is quadratic in sequence length
quiz.explain: Mechanism facts are durable; leadership claims are perishable — the module's honesty rule.

quiz.q: Multi-head attention's purpose is to let the model:
choices: Attend to different representation subspaces at different positions simultaneously
Eliminate the need for training data
quiz.explain: Each head learns different attention patterns (syntax, coreference, position) in parallel subspaces; concatenating them gives richer representations. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Positional information enters a vanilla transformer via:
choices: Positional encodings added to embeddings, since attention is permutation-invariant
quiz.explain: Attention treats its input as a set — without positional encodings the model cannot tell word order. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A causal mask in a decoder ensures:
choices: Each position attends only to earlier positions — no peeking at the future
quiz.explain: Causality is what makes the model a proper generative model: predictions at step t use only tokens before t. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The module's safest long-term claim about architectures is:
choices: Architectural details churn; scaling, data, and evaluation discipline persist — bet on the durable layers
quiz.explain: The module's honesty note: architectures are the fastest-decaying knowledge; the durable lessons are scaling behavior and honest evals. (Frontier honesty.)

modules.title: Quantum Computing Basics
modules.summary: Qubits, superposition, entanglement, and the gate model — what quantum computers are, what they aren't, and where the field stands. As of October 2026.
objectives: Describe a qubit and how it differs from a bit
Explain superposition and entanglement operationally
Name the landmark algorithms and what they actually speed up
State the field's honest status: NISQ era, error correction frontier

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: A **qubit** is a two-level quantum system: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with |α|²+|β|² = 1. **Superposition** is not 'both values at once' in a classical sense — it is a new kind of state whose measurement statistics follow the Born rule. n qubits live in a 2ⁿ-dimensional state space: that exponentiality is the resource — and the reason simulation is hard.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: **Entanglement**: correlations between qubits stronger than any classical correlation (Bell's theorem, experimentally confirmed — Nobel Prize 2022: Aspect, Clauser, Zeilinger). The **gate model** applies unitary operations (Hadamard, CNOT, phase gates); measurement collapses to classical bits. Algorithms are interference choreography: amplify right answers, cancel wrong ones.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **Shor's** (1994): exponential speedup for factoring/discrete log — threatens RSA/ECC *when* large fault-tolerant machines exist. **Grover's** (1996): quadratic speedup for unstructured search. Quantum simulation (Feynman's original 1982 motivation) remains the most plausible near-term scientific win. Claims beyond these need scrutiny — most 'quantum advantage' demos are narrow and contested.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: The field is in the **NISQ** era (noisy intermediate-scale quantum): hundreds–thousands of physical qubits, high error rates. **Fault tolerance** via quantum error correction (surface codes and successors) needs roughly 10³–10⁴ physical qubits per logical qubit — the central engineering mountain. Timelines for cryptographically relevant machines are expert-disputed; treat any date as a claim, not a fact.

cards.back: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩+β|1⟩, |α|²+|β|²=1; measurement follows the Born rule.

cards.front: Why is n-qubit simulation hard classically?
cards.back: The state space is 2ⁿ-dimensional — exponential in n.
Shor: exponential (factoring/discrete log). Grover: quadratic (unstructured search).
Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum — current era: many physical qubits, high errors, no fault tolerance yet.
~10³–10⁴ physical qubits per logical qubit — the central engineering challenge.

cards.front: Superposition vs. entanglement, one line each.
cards.back: Superposition: a qubit can be in a combination of |0⟩ and |1⟩ until measured. Entanglement: two qubits can share a joint state that cannot be factored into individual states — measuring one instantly constrains the other. Both are resources; neither is 'trying all answers at once.' (Concepts.)

Qubits leak information to their environment, collapsing delicate quantum states into classical noise. Decoherence sets the clock: every computation must finish before it wins. Error correction is the plan to fight it — at the cost of many physical qubits per logical qubit. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Quantum advantage vs. quantum supremacy — the terminology.
cards.back: Supremacy: a quantum device performs some task no classical computer feasibly can (the 2019 Sycamore claim, on a contrived sampling task). Advantage: the same, but for a useful task. The honest status as of 2026: supremacy demonstrated on contrived tasks; advantage on useful ones still pending. (Frontier honesty.)

quiz.q: Bell's theorem (Nobel 2022) established:
choices: Quantum correlations exceeding any classical explanation
quiz.explain: Aspect, Clauser, Zeilinger confirmed entanglement's non-classical correlations experimentally.

quiz.q: Shor's algorithm threatens RSA because it:
choices: Factors efficiently on a large fault-tolerant quantum computer
quiz.explain: The threat is real but conditional on fault-tolerant scale — which does not yet exist.

quiz.q: A quantum gate must be:
choices: Unitary (reversible); measurement is the irreversible step
quiz.explain: Computation is unitary evolution; only measurement collapses to classical outcomes.

quiz.q: The most defensible near-term application:
quiz.explain: Feynman's 1982 motivation — simulating quantum systems with quantum systems — remains the plausible first win.

quiz.q: Measuring a qubit in superposition yields:
choices: One classical bit — the superposition collapses to a single outcome
quiz.explain: Measurement collapses superposition to one outcome with probabilities given by the amplitudes — you get one bit out. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Quantum error correction's core cost is:
choices: Many physical qubits per logical qubit — overhead ratios in the hundreds to thousands
quiz.explain: Protecting one logical qubit takes a small army of physical ones; the overhead is the mountain between NISQ and fault tolerance. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Grover's algorithm gives what speedup for unstructured search?
quiz.explain: Grover is quadratic, not exponential — meaningful, but not the RSA-breaking kind. Keep the two algorithms' speedups straight. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The conservative reading of quantum-computing timelines is:
choices: Real progress on error correction and qubit counts, but timelines to cryptographically relevant machines remain measured in years and uncertain
quiz.explain: The module's honesty posture: track error rates and logical-qubit milestones; distrust date-certain predictions. (Frontier honesty.)

modules.title: CRISPR & Gene Editing
modules.summary: How CRISPR-Cas9 works, what base and prime editing add, and where therapeutic gene editing stands — with the ethics up front. As of October 2026.
objectives: Explain the CRISPR-Cas9 mechanism
Distinguish base editing and prime editing
Name approved/sanctioned therapeutic uses as of 2026
Discuss germline vs. somatic editing ethics

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: **CRISPR-Cas9**: a guide RNA (~20 nt) directs the Cas9 nuclease to a complementary DNA sequence adjacent to a **PAM** site; Cas9 makes a double-strand break. The cell's repair — error-prone NHEJ (knockout) or HDR with a template (precise edit) — does the rest. (Doudna/Charpentier, 2012; Nobel 2020.) It is programmable cut-and-paste for genomes — with off-target cuts as the central safety concern.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: **Base editors** (2016–): deaminase fused to nickase-Cas9 — chemically convert one base to another (C→T, A→G) without double-strand breaks. **Prime editing** (2019): nickase fused to reverse transcriptase writes longer edits from an RNA template. Both reduce reliance on double-strand breaks — the field's direction is *precision without breakage*.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: The first CRISPR therapy — **Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel)** for sickle-cell disease and beta thalassemia — was approved in late 2023 (UK/US), an *ex vivo* edit of patients' own blood stem cells. In-vivo programs (e.g., for transthyretin amyloidosis, hereditary angioedema) were in trials. This is the honest frontier: real approvals exist, most applications remain investigational — check current trial registries before citing.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: **Somatic** editing (treated patient's body cells) is broadly accepted under regulation. **Germline** editing (heritable) remains widely condemned after He's 2018 CRISPR-babies case — international consensus (summits 2015, 2018, 2023) holds the line at no clinical germline editing. The ethical frontier: equitable access to million-dollar cures, and enhancement vs. therapy boundaries.

cards.back: Guide RNA directs Cas9 to a PAM-adjacent target; double-strand break; cell repair (NHEJ/HDR) makes the edit.
Base: single-letter chemical conversion, no DSB. Prime: reverse-transcriptase writes longer edits from RNA template.
Ex vivo CRISPR therapy for sickle-cell/beta-thalassemia; approved late 2023 (UK/US) — first CRISPR approval.
Somatic: regulated acceptance. Germline: international consensus against clinical use (post-2018).
Off-target cuts/edits — the field's precision drive targets exactly this.

cards.front: How was CRISPR found? (the history in brief)
cards.back: Microbiologists noticed odd repeating sequences in bacterial genomes (1987 onward); they turned out to be a bacterial immune memory of past viruses, with Cas proteins as the scissors. Doudna and Charpentier (2012) repurposed it as a programmable editor — basic research with no application in mind; Nobel Prize 2020. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Off-target effects: the problem and the mitigations.
cards.back: Cas9 sometimes cuts where the guide RNA nearly matches — off-target edits. Mitigations: high-fidelity Cas variants, better guide design, base and prime editors that avoid double-strand breaks, and whole-genome off-target screening before therapy. Safety is measured, not assumed. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Germline vs. somatic: the bright line and its status.
cards.back: Somatic edits affect only the patient; germline edits are heritable. The scientific consensus (and law in most countries): somatic therapy is proceeding; heritable editing is off-limits — the 2018 He Jiankui case drew universal condemnation and a prison sentence. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Cas9 needs, in addition to guide-RNA complementarity:
choices: A PAM site adjacent to the target
quiz.explain: The protospacer-adjacent motif licenses cutting — a key specificity determinant.

quiz.q: NHEJ vs. HDR after the cut:
choices: NHEnd joining: error-prone knockout; HDR: template-precise edit
quiz.explain: The repair pathway decides the outcome — most therapeutic strategies wrestle with this.

quiz.q: Prime editing's advantage over standard Cas9:
choices: Longer precise edits without double-strand breaks
quiz.explain: Nickase + reverse transcriptase writes from a template — precision without breakage.

quiz.q: The 2018 He Jiankui case concerned:
choices: Heritable (germline) editing of babies — globally condemned
quiz.explain: The case that hardened the international line against clinical germline editing.

quiz.q: The PAM sequence matters because:
choices: Cas9 requires it adjacent to the target to bind and cut — the enzyme's landing check
quiz.explain: No PAM, no cut — the protospacer-adjacent motif is Cas9's required context signal. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Base editing differs from standard CRISPR-Cas9 in that it:
choices: Chemically converts one base to another without a double-strand break
quiz.explain: Base editors deaminate the target base in place — no break, no donor template, fewer indels. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Casgevy (2023) is significant as:
choices: The first CRISPR-based therapy approved — for sickle cell disease and beta thalassemia
quiz.explain: FDA approval December 2023: ex vivo editing of patients' own stem cells — the proof that CRISPR therapy reached the clinic. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The most honest summary of CRISPR therapeutics as of 2026 is:
choices: Cures for all genetic disease are here
A real, approved platform for a few blood disorders, with delivery — getting editors into the right cells in the body — as the binding constraint
quiz.explain: Ex vivo blood-disorder therapies work; in vivo delivery to solid tissues is the frontier. Date-stamped and conservative. (Frontier honesty.)

modules.title: Fusion Energy Status
modules.summary: Magnetic vs. inertial confinement, the NIF ignition milestone, private fusion's surge — and why grid power remains the mountain. As of October 2026.
objectives: Explain the two confinement approaches
State what NIF's ignition did and didn't prove
Name the leading private efforts and their approaches
Give the honest timeline framing

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: **Magnetic confinement** (tokamaks, stellarators): hold a 100M°C plasma with magnetic fields — ITER (France, international) is the giant; stellarators (Wendelstein 7-X) trade engineering complexity for steadier plasma. **Inertial confinement**: crush fuel pellets with lasers — NIF's approach. Both chase the same figure of merit: **Q**, fusion energy out over heating energy in.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: The National Ignition Facility achieved **scientific breakeven** (December 2022, repeated since): fusion output exceeded laser energy delivered to the target. What it did *not* prove: wall-plug breakeven (lasers are inefficient), repetition rate (NIF fires ~daily; power needs ~10/second), or economics. A physics milestone, not an energy milestone — the distinction matters.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Since ~2020, private capital flooded in: **Commonwealth Fusion Systems** (tokamak + high-temperature superconducting magnets), **Helion** (pulsed magneto-inertial, aiming direct electricity conversion), **TAE**, **General Fusion**, and others — collectively billions raised. HTS magnets are the enabling technology story: stronger fields ⇒ smaller, cheaper tokamaks. Company timelines cluster optimistically; treat them as targets.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: 'Fusion is 30 years away' is a joke with a point: the physics keeps progressing (ignition was real) while *grid electricity* needs Q≫1 at the wall plug, materials surviving neutron bombardment, tritium breeding, and cost-competitive $/MWh. Progress is genuine; power-plant timelines remain expert-disputed. Date every claim.

cards.back: Magnetic: tokamaks/stellarators hold hot plasma in fields. Inertial: lasers crush pellets (NIF).
Fusion energy out / heating energy in — the figure of merit.

cards.front: What did NIF 2022 prove — and not prove?
cards.back: Scientific breakeven (target gain > 1), repeated. Not: wall-plug gain, rep rate, economics.
Stronger fields ⇒ smaller/cheaper tokamaks — the private-fusion enabling story (CFS et al.).

cards.front: The four mountains to grid power?
cards.back: Wall-plug Q, neutron-surviving materials, tritium breeding, competitive $/MWh.

cards.front: The Lawson criterion in plain words.
cards.back: The triple product — temperature × density × confinement time — must exceed a threshold for fusion to self-sustain. Magnetic and inertial approaches attack different terms: tokamaks push confinement time, NIF pushes density. One number, two strategies. (Concepts.)

D–T fusion (the easiest reaction) needs tritium, which barely exists naturally (12-year half-life) and must be bred from lithium in the reactor blanket. Every D–T power-plant design is also a tritium factory — a breeding ratio above 1 is a requirement, not a bonus. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Fusion vs. fission: the honest comparison.
cards.back: Fusion fuel is abundant and its waste shorter-lived, but the physics is far harder — containing hundred-million-degree plasma versus sustaining a chain reaction. Fission powers grids today; fusion's grid contribution as of 2026 is zero. Compare realities, not press releases. (Frontier honesty.)

quiz.q: ITER is an example of:
quiz.explain: The world's largest tokamak experiment, under construction in France.

quiz.q: NIF's ignition means fusion power plants are:
choices: Proven at the physics level; engineering/economics unproven
quiz.explain: Target gain > 1 is real physics; everything about power plants remains ahead.

quiz.q: A stellarator differs from a tokamak mainly in:
choices: Magnetic geometry — steadier plasma at higher engineering complexity
quiz.explain: Wendelstein 7-X: twisted coils shape the field without tokamak plasma current.

quiz.q: Helion's distinctive bet:
choices: Pulsed magneto-inertial fusion with direct electricity conversion
quiz.explain: Skipping the steam cycle — if it works, a different economics entirely.

quiz.q: NIF's 2022 ignition demonstrated:
choices: Scientific breakeven in a single implosion — more fusion energy out than laser energy in — not a path to grid power
quiz.explain: Ignition is a physics milestone: the implosion produced more fusion energy than the lasers delivered to the target. Wall-plug efficiency and repetition rate are separate mountains. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A tokamak confines plasma using:
choices: Magnetic fields in a toroidal chamber
quiz.explain: Tokamak = toroidal magnetic confinement; the plasma never touches the walls. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Private fusion companies' main strategic bet is:
choices: Smaller, faster-iterated designs (often with HTS magnets) reaching milestones sooner than ITER-scale projects
quiz.explain: The private surge bets that high-temperature superconducting magnets and faster build cycles compress the timeline — unproven at grid scale, but a real strategic thesis. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The module's 'four mountains' framing says grid fusion requires:
choices: Ignition physics, materials surviving neutron flux, tritium breeding, and economic electricity — all four, in sequence
quiz.explain: Physics was mountain one; engineering, fuel cycle, and economics remain. Single-breakthrough narratives fail this checklist. (Frontier honesty.)

modules.title: Brain–Computer Interfaces
modules.summary: Invasive vs. non-invasive BCIs, what decoding actually achieves today, and the clinical frontier — plus the neuroethics. As of October 2026.
objectives: Distinguish invasive, semi-invasive, and non-invasive BCIs
Describe what neural decoding can and cannot do today
Name the clinical applications in trials
Raise the core neuroethical questions

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: **Non-invasive** (EEG, fNIRS): scalp signals — safe, but centimeters of skull blur everything; good for coarse control. **Semi-invasive** (ECoG): electrodes on the brain surface — better signal, requires surgery. **Invasive** (Utah arrays, Neuralink-style threads): single-neuron resolution, highest bandwidth, highest risk. The trade is always **bandwidth vs. invasiveness**.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: Motor BCIs let paralyzed users move cursors and robotic arms by decoded intent; **speech neuroprostheses** reconstruct intended speech from motor cortex at improving rates (2021–2024 papers showed striking progress). What it is *not*: mind reading — decoding works on trained tasks with cooperating subjects and heavy ML; 'thought extraction' headlines outrun the science by miles.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Trials target paralysis (motor/speech restoration), with companies (Neuralink, Synchron, Precision Neuroscience, Paradromics) and academic labs pushing implant counts and longevity. The honest state: genuine restored function for some patients, early days for scale — electrode longevity, surgical risk, and regulatory pathways are the binding constraints, not just decoding algorithms.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: BCIs raise questions other tech doesn't: **mental privacy** (neural data is the most intimate data class), **agency** (who authored a decoded action?), **consent** for locked-in patients, and **enhancement** divides. The field's norm — encode these *before* the capability arrives, per the Collingridge lesson (IL-21). Regulation here is genuinely unsettled; watch it.

cards.back: Non-invasive (EEG: safe, coarse) → ECoG (surface, surgery) → invasive (single-neuron, highest bandwidth/risk).
Bandwidth vs. invasiveness — always.
Reconstructing intended speech from motor cortex; rapid progress 2021–2024; trained tasks, cooperating subjects.
Mind reading — decoding needs training, cooperation, and heavy ML on specific tasks.
Mental privacy, agency/authorship of decoded actions, consent — plus enhancement divides.

cards.front: The Utah array: what it is, and its limits.
cards.back: A 4×4 mm silicon grid of 100 penetrating microelectrodes — the workhorse of human intracortical BCI research since the 2000s. Limits: scarring degrades signals over years, it samples a tiny patch of cortex, and implantation is brain surgery. The gold standard and the cautionary tale in one device. (Concepts.)

Synchron's stent-like electrode array delivered via blood vessels — no open-brain surgery. Lower signal quality than penetrating arrays, but dramatically lower surgical risk. The trade ladder in one device: invasiveness for bandwidth, explicitly priced. (Concepts.)

Mapping recorded neural activity to intended outputs (cursor movement, attempted speech) via trained models — pattern recognition on brain signals, not mind reading. Performance is impressive in constrained tasks and brittle outside them. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: ECoG sits between EEG and Utah arrays in:
quiz.explain: Surface electrodes: surgery required, but far better signal than scalp EEG.

quiz.q: A headline claims 'AI reads minds.' The informed response:
choices: Decoding works on trained tasks with cooperating subjects — far from general mind reading
quiz.explain: The honest position credits real progress while rejecting the extrapolation.

quiz.q: The binding constraints on clinical BCI scale are:
choices: Electrode longevity, surgical risk, regulation — not just decoding
quiz.explain: Implants must survive years in the body and clear regulators — hardware and policy, not just ML.

quiz.q: Neural data deserves special protection because:
choices: It's the most intimate data class — mental privacy
quiz.explain: The neuroethical core: thoughts-adjacent data needs a higher bar.

quiz.q: EEG's fundamental limitation for BCI is:
choices: Spatial resolution — skull and scalp smear the signal
quiz.explain: EEG is non-invasive and cheap, but the skull blurs electrical fields — great for timing, poor for locating. The ladder's bottom rung. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Speech neuroprostheses (as of 2026) have demonstrated:
choices: Decoding attempted speech at useful rates in clinical-trial participants with paralysis — real, narrow, early
quiz.explain: Published results show dozens of words per minute from attempted speech in locked-in patients. A genuine milestone; not telepathy. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The binding constraints on scaling clinical BCI are:
choices: Surgical risk, signal longevity, and regulatory burden — not decoder algorithms
quiz.explain: The algorithms are ahead of the interfaces: safe, durable, approved implants are the bottleneck. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Neural data deserves special protection because:
choices: It is intimately linked to identity, intent, and health — and unlike a password, you cannot rotate your cortex
quiz.explain: Non-revocable, identity-bearing, health-revealing: the strongest case in the module for data exceptionalism. (Frontier honesty.)

modules.title: AI Agents & Inference-Time Compute
modules.summary: From chatbots to agents: tool use, planning loops, and the shift from training-time to inference-time scaling. As of October 2026.
objectives: Describe the agent loop: perceive, plan, act, observe
Explain tool use and function calling
State the inference-time scaling thesis
Name the evaluation and safety challenges

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: An **AI agent** wraps a model in a loop: observe state → reason/plan → **act via tools** (APIs, code execution, browsers) → observe results → repeat. The model supplies the policy; the scaffolding supplies memory, tools, and persistence. Capabilities come from the *system*, not the weights alone — which is why evals must test systems, not just models.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: **Function calling / tool use**: the model emits structured calls (JSON schemas), the harness executes them and returns observations. This grounds models in live data and real actions — and creates the attack surface: **prompt injection** (malicious instructions in tool outputs) is the signature vulnerability of the agent era. Treat every tool output as untrusted data.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: The post-2024 thesis: capability also scales with **compute spent at inference** — longer chains of thought, sampling many candidates, search and verification, multi-agent debate. 'Test-time compute' became a second scaling axis alongside training compute. The economics flip: intelligence becomes *runnable* cost, and latency/cost budgets become design parameters.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: Agent evals are genuinely hard: long-horizon tasks, nondeterminism, and environments that fight back. Benchmarks saturate; real deployment surprises persist. Safety work focuses on **containment** (least-privilege tools, human approval gates), **monitoring** (action logs, anomaly detection), and **alignment** of the planner itself. The frontier moves too fast for settled textbooks — read primary sources.

cards.back: Observe → plan → act via tools → observe → repeat; model = policy, scaffolding = memory/tools/persistence.
Malicious instructions embedded in tool outputs/data — the signature vulnerability of tool-using agents.
Capability scales with compute spent at inference (longer reasoning, sampling, search) — a second scaling axis.

cards.front: Why evals must test systems, not models?
cards.back: Capability lives in model + scaffolding + tools; weights-alone benchmarks miss it.
Containment (least privilege, approval gates), monitoring (logs, anomaly detection), planner alignment.

cards.front: ReAct pattern: the loop in words.
cards.back: Reason + Act: the model interleaves thought traces with tool calls — think, act, observe, repeat. The 2022 paper's simple loop became the skeleton of nearly every agent framework: reasoning guides tool use, tool outputs ground reasoning. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Tool-use failure modes: the big three.
cards.back: Hallucinated tool calls (invoking tools that don't exist), argument errors (right tool, malformed input), and untrusted tool output (prompt injection via tool returns). Agent reliability engineering is mostly taming these three. (Concepts.)

End-to-end task completion in sandboxed environments (SWE-bench, RE-Bench, METR's suites) — can the system do the job, not just answer questions about it. The module's insistence: evals must test systems with tools, because tools change the capability profile completely. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Function calling works by:
choices: The model browsing the web freely
Structured calls (schemas) executed by the harness, observations returned
quiz.explain: JSON-schema calls the model emits; the system executes and feeds back results.

quiz.q: Prompt injection is dangerous because:
choices: Tool outputs are data, but the model may treat embedded text as instructions
quiz.explain: The data/instruction boundary collapses — untrusted content steering a trusted agent.

quiz.q: Inference-time compute trades:
choices: Latency and cost for capability — intelligence as runnable cost
quiz.explain: The economic flip: you can buy smarter answers per query.

quiz.q: The hardest part of agent evaluation:
choices: Long horizons, nondeterminism, adversarial environments; benchmarks saturate
quiz.explain: Real deployment keeps surprising saturated benchmarks — eval science lags capability.

quiz.q: In a ReAct loop, the 'observation' is:
choices: The result returned by the environment or tool after an action
quiz.explain: Thought → Action → Observation: the loop grounds reasoning in real tool outputs. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The 'inference-time scaling' thesis claims capability also grows with:
choices: Compute spent at inference — longer reasoning chains, more samples, search
quiz.explain: The post-2024 finding: spending compute at test time (extended reasoning, best-of-N sampling) buys capability the way training compute did. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A benchmark that tests only the bare model, without tools, will:
choices: Underestimate what the deployed system can do — tools are part of the capability
quiz.explain: Capability lives in the system (model + tools + scaffolding); model-only evals miss it. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The most defensible near-term agent-safety posture is:
choices: Layered: capability evals, deployment monitoring, and kill-switches — defense in depth, honestly scoped
quiz.explain: No single layer suffices; the module advocates measured, layered controls — neither apocalyptic nor complacent framing. (Frontier honesty.)

modules.title: Semiconductor Scaling Beyond Moore
modules.summary: Where Moore's law stands, what replaced it (chiplets, 3D stacking, new lithography), and why compute is the strategic resource. As of October 2026.
objectives: State Moore's law and its current status
Explain chiplets, 3D stacking, and advanced packaging
Describe EUV lithography's role
Connect compute to AI progress economics

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: **Moore's law** (1965): transistor counts doubling ~every 2 years. The *economic* version (cheaper transistors) slowed around the mid-2010s as fabs hit atomic and economic limits; the *density* version continues via 3D structures (FinFET → gate-all-around). 'Moore's law is dead' and 'alive' are both slogans — the truth: single-thread scaling ended (~2005, the power wall), density scaling continues expensively.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: **Chiplets**: compose big chips from small dies (better yields, mix-and-match process nodes) — AMD's bet, now industry standard. **3D stacking** (HBM memory stacks, hybrid bonding): bandwidth through the vertical dimension. **Advanced packaging** (CoWoS and successors) is now as strategic as lithography — the bottleneck for AI accelerators is packaging capacity, not just wafers.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: **EUV** (extreme ultraviolet, 13.5nm) lithography — ASML's machines, each the most complex mass-produced artifact in history — enabled sub-10nm nodes. **High-NA EUV** is the next step (finer features, eye-watering cost). One Dutch company holding the keys to the frontier is itself a geopolitical fact.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: AI progress now visibly tracks **compute**: training runs measured in tens of thousands of accelerators, datacenters as the new factories. Export controls on advanced chips (US, from 2022) made semiconductors an instrument of statecraft. For the technologist: performance engineering increasingly means *parallelism and memory hierarchy*, not waiting for faster cores.

cards.back: Transistor doubling ~2yr (1965). Single-thread scaling ended ~2005; density continues expensively; economic doubling slowed ~2010s.
Chiplets: small dies composed (yields, node mixing). 3D: vertical integration (HBM) for bandwidth.
13.5nm lithography enabling sub-10nm (ASML); High-NA = finer features, next step.
CoWoS-class capacity bottlenecks AI accelerators — packaging rivals lithography in importance.
Parallelism + memory hierarchy, not faster cores — the power wall ended free single-thread gains.

cards.front: Dennard scaling: what broke, and when.
cards.back: Dennard (1974): as transistors shrink, power density stays constant — smaller meant faster AND cooler. It broke around 2005–2006 (the power wall): leakage current stopped shrinking, ending clock-speed growth and forcing the multicore turn. (Concepts.)

Numerical aperture 0.33 → 0.55: finer features per exposure, fewer multi-patterning steps — at the cost of enormous, expensive tools that only one company (ASML) builds. Lithography's frontier is now as much about economics as physics. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Why memory bandwidth, not just FLOPS, gates AI training.
cards.back: GPUs starve waiting for data: training throughput is bounded by how fast weights and activations move, not just multiply. Hence HBM stacks, NVLink fabrics, and the industry's obsession with interconnect — the memory wall is the binding constraint. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The 'power wall' (~2005) ended:
choices: Free single-thread performance gains from frequency scaling
quiz.explain: Dennard scaling broke; clocks stalled; the industry went multicore.

quiz.q: Chiplets improve economics mainly via:
choices: Better yields on small dies + mixing process nodes
quiz.explain: Small dies dodge defect statistics; logic and I/O can use different nodes.

quiz.q: HBM (high-bandwidth memory) achieves bandwidth through:
quiz.explain: Vertical stacking + wide interfaces — the memory wall's current answer.

quiz.q: US chip export controls (from 2022) show:
choices: Compute is an instrument of statecraft
quiz.explain: Advanced semiconductors became geopolitical — strategy, not just supply chain.

quiz.q: Moore's law, precisely stated, is about:
choices: Transistor density doubling roughly every two years — an economic observation, not a physical law
quiz.explain: Moore (1965) described an economic-technological cadence; treating it as physics is the category error the module warns against. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The multicore turn (~2005) was caused by:
choices: The power wall ending frequency scaling — performance had to come from parallelism
quiz.explain: When clocks stopped rising, architects spent the transistor budget on cores instead. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A chiplet design's main economic win is:
choices: Yield — small dies have fewer killer defects, so more good chips per wafer
quiz.explain: Defect math: halving die area more than halves the chance a defect kills the die. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Export controls on advanced chips (from 2022) demonstrate that:
choices: Compute is strategic infrastructure — states now treat leading-edge chips like oil or uranium
quiz.explain: The module's 'compute as strategy' note: leading compute is now an instrument of statecraft. (Frontier honesty.)

modules.title: Synthetic Biology
modules.summary: Engineering biology: DNA synthesis and sequencing economics, the design-build-test-learn loop, and what biofoundries actually produce. As of October 2026.
objectives: Explain the DBTL loop
State the cost trajectories of sequencing and synthesis
Name real synbio products and platforms
Raise biosecurity as the field's Collingridge problem

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: **Sequencing** cost fell ~100,000× since 2007 (faster than Moore's law for a decade) — a human genome now costs hundreds of dollars. **Synthesis** (writing DNA) fell slower but steadily; gene-length synthesis is routine, genome-scale writing remains heroic. The gap matters: reading is cheap, writing is the frontier.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: **Design–Build–Test–Learn**: specify a genetic construct, synthesize/assemble it, test in cells, learn from data — the engineering cycle applied to biology. **Biofoundries** automate it (liquid handling, high-throughput screening). Biology's version of the compile-run-debug loop, with evolution as the legacy codebase.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Real products: engineered **insulin** and biologics (the old wins), **bio-based materials** (spider-silk proteins, mycelium), **fermentation-produced** chemicals displacing petrochemistry, **cell therapies** (CAR-T). mRNA vaccines (2020) proved the platform logic: *programmable* biology. Most synbio revenue is still tools and services — the application layer is early.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: The Collingridge problem in a lab coat: synthesis screening, the **Australia Group** lists, and debates over publishing methods of concern. As capabilities diffuse, governance leans on **screening synthesis orders** and norms — imperfect, evolving, and genuinely contested. The field's social license depends on getting this visibly right.

cards.back: Sequencing: ~100,000× cheaper since 2007. Synthesis: falling, slower — writing is the frontier.
Design–Build–Test–Learn: specify, synthesize, test in cells, learn — biology's compile-run-debug.
Biologics/cell therapies, bio-materials (silk proteins, mycelium), fermentation chemicals.
Platform logic proven: programmable biology can answer in months, not decades.
Synthesis-order screening, control lists, publication norms — imperfect, evolving, contested.

Biology reads DNA→RNA→protein; synbio writes it: design a sequence, synthesize it, boot it up in a cell. Reading (sequencing) got cheap first; writing (synthesis) is catching up — the module's core asymmetry. (Concepts.)

Patient T-cells reprogrammed with a synthetic receptor to hunt cancer — approved therapies (2017 onward) with real remissions. Not CRISPR per se, but the proof that engineered living cells are medicine. (Concepts.)

cards.front: The 'playing God' objection: the module's honest handling.
cards.back: The module neither dismisses nor endorses: it distinguishes the technical question (can we do it safely?) from the worldview question (should we?), and notes that every prior biotechnology — from fermentation to IVF — faced the same objection and was decided case by case. (Frontier honesty.)

quiz.q: A human genome sequence in 2026 costs roughly:
quiz.explain: The ~$1,000 genome arrived in the 2010s; costs kept falling into the hundreds.

quiz.q: The DBTL loop's 'Learn' step uses:
choices: Data from the Test step to improve the next Design
quiz.explain: The loop is iterative — measured performance feeds redesign.

quiz.q: Genome-scale DNA writing remains 'heroic' because:
choices: Synthesis cost and error rates scale badly with length
quiz.explain: Writing long perfect DNA is still expensive and error-prone — the synthesis frontier.

quiz.q: Synthesis screening exists to:
choices: Catch orders for sequences of concern — biosecurity
quiz.explain: DNA synthesis providers screen against pathogen lists — the governance layer.

quiz.q: Gibson assembly and commercial DNA synthesis let engineers:
choices: Write arbitrary DNA sequences — the 'writing' half of synbio
quiz.explain: Synthesis is writing: specifying a sequence and having it built. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The DBTL loop's 'Test' step typically involves:
choices: High-throughput measurement — sequencing, mass spec, plate readers — generating data for the Learn step
quiz.explain: Test is measurement at scale; without it the loop has no error signal. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The mRNA-vaccine lesson for synbio is:
choices: A programmable platform (swap the sequence, keep the delivery system) beats bespoke development — speed comes from the platform
quiz.explain: Same lipid nanoparticle, new payload: the platform economics that made 2020's speed possible. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Synthesis screening's purpose is:
choices: Keeping dangerous sequences (pathogens, toxins) out of synthesized DNA — the biosecurity gate
quiz.explain: Providers screen orders against pathogen databases; it is the industry's front-line biosecurity control. (Frontier honesty.)

modules.title: Space Infrastructure
modules.summary: Reusable launch economics, megaconstellations, and the cislunar horizon — space as infrastructure, not spectacle. As of October 2026.
objectives: Explain the reusable-launch cost revolution
Describe megaconstellations as infrastructure
Outline the cislunar/Artemis program
Name the orbital-debris problem honestly

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: **SpaceX's Falcon 9** (first booster landing 2015) cut orbital launch costs roughly an order of magnitude — from ~$10,000/kg toward ~$1,000/kg-class economics. **Starship** (fully reusable, super-heavy) aims for another order of magnitude; as of 2026 it was flying test and early operational missions with full rapid reusability still in work. The lesson: *reusability*, not new physics, moved the curve.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: **Starlink** (thousands of satellites, operational since 2020) proved LEO broadband at scale — latency and coverage impossible for GEO. Competitors (OneWeb, Kuiper) follow. Consequences: astronomy's light-pollution fight, spectrum/orbit coordination crises, and a genuine connectivity layer for remote regions. Infrastructure has side effects — always.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: NASA's **Artemis** program targets sustained lunar presence (Gateway station, surface missions) with commercial landers; China pursues parallel lunar plans (ILRS). The strategic logic: the Moon as proving ground and resource base (water ice → propellant). Timelines have slipped repeatedly — date every claim, and distinguish funded hardware from renderings.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: Tens of thousands of tracked objects, millions of lethal-but-untracked fragments; the **Kessler syndrome** (collisional cascade) is the tail risk. Megaconstellations multiply the conjunction load. Active debris removal is demonstrated in pieces, not at scale. The honest framing: orbit is a commons, and commons need governance — currently thin.

cards.back: Reusable booster (landings from 2015) cut $/kg roughly 10× — reusability, not new physics.
Fully reusable super-heavy lift; another order-of-magnitude cost cut — rapid reusability still in work as of 2026.

cards.front: Why LEO beats GEO for broadband?
cards.back: Latency: ~500km vs ~36,000km altitude — physics, not marketing.
Sustained lunar presence; Moon as proving ground + resource base (water → propellant).
Collisional cascade: debris collisions breeding more debris — the orbital tail risk.

cards.front: Why is propellant the real currency of spaceflight?
cards.back: The rocket equation: every maneuver costs mass exponentially. Lunar water ice matters because it can become propellant (split to hydrogen and oxygen) at the top of Earth's gravity well — a gas station changes the economics of the whole inner solar system. (Concepts.)

cards.front: GEO vs. LEO vs. MEO: the trade in one pass.
cards.back: GEO (35,786 km): fixed over one spot, high latency (~600 ms), great for broadcast. LEO (~550 km): low latency, needs thousands of satellites for coverage — the Starlink architecture. MEO: the GPS compromise. Orbit is a latency/coverage/cost trade. (Concepts.)

cards.front: The Artemis Accords: what they are.
cards.back: US-led bilateral agreements (30+ signatories as of 2026) setting norms for lunar activity: transparency, interoperability, resource-extraction rights. Not a treaty, not universal — the governance layer being built while the hardware flies. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Falcon 9's cost impact came mainly from:
quiz.explain: Landing and reflying boosters amortized the expensive hardware.

quiz.q: Starlink's key technical enabler:
quiz.explain: The constellation business closes only with low $/kg and satellite mass production.

quiz.q: Lunar water ice matters because:
choices: Propellant feedstock (split to H2/O2) — the cislunar economy's oil
quiz.explain: In-space propellant changes the rocket equation's economics — the strategic prize.

quiz.q: The honest way to read a 2028 lunar-base announcement:
choices: Distinguish funded hardware from renderings; timelines have slipped repeatedly
quiz.explain: Date every claim; hardware talks, renderings walk.

quiz.q: Reusable boosters changed launch economics mainly by:
choices: Amortizing the most expensive hardware over many flights — the booster is most of the cost
quiz.explain: The booster is the expensive part; flying it dozens of times collapses dollars per kilogram. Fuel was always cheap. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Starlink's key technical enabler was:
choices: Cheap, frequent launch plus mass-produced satellites — the constellation is a manufacturing achievement
quiz.explain: The constellation exists because launch got cheap enough to industrialize orbit. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The Kessler syndrome describes:
choices: A debris cascade — collisions generating debris that causes more collisions, potentially closing orbits
quiz.explain: The self-sustaining debris feedback loop; the reason megaconstellation operators deorbit dead satellites. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Reading a '2028 lunar base' announcement honestly means asking:
choices: Which hardware exists, who is funded, and what the critical path is — announcements are not schedules
quiz.explain: The module's method: separate flown hardware from funded plans from aspirations. (Frontier honesty.)

modules.title: The Frontier Method
modules.summary: How to read the fast-moving edge honestly: preprints, benchmarks, hype detection, and the as-of discipline — the meta-skill this academy exists to teach.
objectives: Read a preprint critically in 20 minutes
Detect hype patterns in tech announcements
Apply the as-of discipline to every frontier claim
Maintain a personal frontier radar

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: The protocol: (1) **Abstract + claims** — what exactly is asserted? (2) **Method** — what was actually done, on what data, with what controls? (3) **Results vs. claims** — do the figures support the abstract? (4) **Baselines** — were competitors given a fair fight? (5) **Limitations** — stated or conspicuous by absence? (6) **Provenance** — who wrote it, what's their incentive? Most papers fail at step 3 or 4.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: Watch for: **benchmark cherry-picking** (one metric, friendly settings); **the demo/data gap** (works on stage, untested in the wild); **category errors** ('quantum' + 'consciousness'); **timeline laundering** (a target quoted as a fact); **authority borrowing** (a famous name, no relevant expertise); **the inevitable graph** (exponential pasted onto a noisy series). Each has a question that kills it — learn the questions.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Every frontier claim gets a **date** and a **half-life estimate**: mechanism facts (years), product claims (months), leadership claims (weeks). Write 'as of <date>' reflexively. When you cite a frontier fact older than its half-life, re-verify or qualify. This academy's modules carry asOf fields for exactly this reason — and the daily pipeline keeps them fresh.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: Maintain: 2–3 **primary sources** (arXiv categories, conference proceedings), 1 **aggregator** you trust, 1 **skeptic** who is usually right, and a **claim log** — predictions with dates, revisited quarterly. The log is the instrument: it converts consumption into calibration. The frontier rewards the calibrated, not the first.

cards.back: Claims → method → results-vs-claims → baselines → limitations → provenance.

cards.front: Name four hype patterns and their killing questions.
cards.back: Cherry-picking (which metrics were omitted?); demo/data gap (tested in the wild?); timeline laundering (target or fact?); authority borrowing (relevant expertise?).
Date every claim; estimate its half-life (mechanism: years; product: months; leadership: weeks); re-verify past half-life.
2–3 primary sources, 1 trusted aggregator, 1 good skeptic, and a dated claim log revisited quarterly.

cards.front: Why does the claim log matter?
cards.back: It converts consumption into calibration — the frontier rewards the calibrated, not the first.

After abstract and figures, read methods before conclusions: the methods tell you what was actually done, and half of all hype dies there — wrong baseline, tiny sample, metric gaming. Conclusions are marketing; methods are the audit trail. (Concepts.)

Before updating on the exciting new result, ask: how often do claims of this type pan out? (Most 'breakthrough' press releases don't.) Base rates anchor you against vivid anecdotes — the single most useful habit in the module. (Concepts.)

cards.front: The claim log: format and purpose.
cards.back: One line per claim: date, source, exact assertion, your confidence, expiry or review date. Purpose: claims are inventory — without a log you cannot tell which of your beliefs are stale, and frontier beliefs go stale fast. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: A paper's abstract claims SOTA; the baselines are two years old. You:
choices: Flag unfair baselines — the claim is unsupported
quiz.explain: Step 4 of the protocol: stale baselines invalidate leadership claims.

quiz.q: 'Quantum AI will be conscious by 2028' exhibits:
quiz.explain: Two hype patterns stacked — consciousness isn't operationalized, and 2028 is a wish.

quiz.q: A frontier fact from 2023 about 'the best open model' should be:
choices: Re-verified or qualified — past its half-life
quiz.explain: Leadership claims have week-scale half-lives; a 2023 claim is archaeology.

quiz.q: The most valuable item in a frontier radar:
quiz.explain: Calibration compounds; speed without calibration is just faster error.

quiz.q: A paper claims SOTA with baselines two years old. The method's verdict:
choices: Discount heavily: stale baselines are a classic hype pattern — the claim is unevaluated until tested against current methods
quiz.explain: Hype pattern: beating yesterday's competition. Check the baselines' dates before the headline. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: 'Scientists baffled' in a headline is a signal to:
choices: Check whether the paper itself makes the modest claim the headline inflates — headline is not the paper
quiz.explain: Headlines optimize for clicks; the paper's own claims section is the ground truth. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The as-of discipline requires every frontier claim to carry:
choices: A date, a source, and an uncertainty — when, from where, how sure
quiz.explain: Date + source + uncertainty: the three tags that keep a fast-moving belief honest. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: The most valuable item in a frontier radar is:
choices: A small set of load-bearing indicators you actually update — depth beats breadth
quiz.explain: A radar you don't update is a museum. Few indicators, regularly refreshed, beat a firehose. (Concepts.)

modules.title: Frontier Capability Forecasting: The Epoch AI Corpus
modules.summary: Welcome to the measurement wing of the Frontier. I'm your instructor for this module, and we're going to do something unusual: instead of learning a technology, we're learning how the frontier learns about itself. Epoch AI is the research group that tracks AI's physical supply chains — data, chips, dollars — and turns those measurements into bounded forecasts of what comes next. In this module you'll reconstruct two of their flagship analyses: the 'data wall' question (will we run out of training data?) and the 'agent capacity' question (how many AI agents could the chip buildout actually run?). Every figure here is dated, because frontier numbers decay — dating them is part of the discipline. All fast-moving claims: as of October 7, 2026.
objectives: Explain Epoch AI's capability-forecasting method: physical inputs (data stocks, chip shipments, cost curves) projected into bounded frontier forecasts
Reconstruct the data-wall argument: scaling-law demand vs. estimated supply, the quality and multi-epoch adjustments, and the 2026-2032 exhaustion window
Reproduce Epoch's agent-capacity estimation (A = E × c) and its key result: ~30-170M concurrent frontier agents from 2025-27 HBM shipments
Interpret inference cost curves (~47%/quarter since 2023) and their budget implications for AI engineering
Apply the decay lesson: why frontier forecasts carry as-of dates and why the binding constraint moves over time

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Capability forecasting** — The research practice of converting unobservable quantities about AI's future — remaining usable training data, deployable agent capacity, the cost of a fixed capability — into bounded forecasts with stated assumptions and uncertainty intervals.
- **The data wall** — The projected point at which training datasets reach the size of the available stock of public human-generated text. Villalobos et al. (2024) place it between 2026 and 2032, median 2028.
- **Neural scaling laws** — Empirical relationships (Kaplan 2020; Hoffmann/Chinchilla 2022) tying optimal dataset size to roughly the square root of training compute — the demand side of the data-wall ledger.
- **Stock estimates** — The paper's Table 1 point estimates of usable text: Common Crawl ~130T tokens, the indexed web ~510T, the whole web ~3100T, images ~300T, video ~1350T (as of the paper, 2024).
- **Quality filtering** — Only a fraction of deduplicated web text is usable without degrading model performance; this adjustment shrinks the effective stock.
- **Multi-epoch training** — Repeat passes over the same data stretch the effective stock by a capped multiplier; this adjustment grows it.
- **Monte Carlo simulation** — The paper propagates parameter uncertainty through repeated random sampling, producing the 2026–2032 window rather than a single year.
- **Agent capacity (A = E × c)** — Epoch's October 2026 estimation: effective hardware supply E (HBM memory shipped 2025–27, expressed in GB300 equivalents) multiplied by serving capacity c (concurrent agent sessions per GB300).
- **GB300 equivalent** — Epoch's unit of account for hardware supply: the HBM capacity of one GB300-class AI server, used to normalize heterogeneous chip shipments.
- **TraceLab / AgentX** — The two concurrency sources in Epoch's report: API spending per agent-hour from the TraceLab dataset of coding-agent session traces (closed models), and SemiAnalysis's AgentX serving benchmarks at fixed streaming speeds (open models).
- **The plunging price of thought** — Epoch's September 2026 finding: the cost of a fixed level of benchmark performance has fallen roughly 47% per quarter — about 13× per year — since 2023.
- **Binding constraint / capacity glut** — The lesson of the agent-capacity report: the scarce resource moved from chips to demand. Using just 20% of central capacity would imply $2.6–5.3T/year in API-equivalent spending (Epoch, 2026-10-02), far above projected developer revenue — a potential capacity glut.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Grab a notebook or a scratch file. We're going to reproduce both of Epoch's headline calculations at the level of a careful reader — not the full Monte Carlo, but every input and where it comes from.
1. **Demand side of the data wall.** Start from the scaling-law rule of thumb: optimal dataset size grows roughly with the square root of training compute. If training compute grows 10×, the dataset that justifies it grows about 3.16×. Compound that across years of compute growth and data demand compounds against a finite stock.
2. **Supply side, raw.** Estimate the indexed web's plain text with the paper's recipe: ~250 billion pages in Google's index (2022 figure) × ~7,000 bytes of plain text per page from Common Crawl statistics → convert bytes to tokens with a byte-pair tokenizer. That is the raw token stock.
3. **Adjust down — quality filtering.** Only a fraction of deduplicated web text trains well. Multiply the raw stock by the usable fraction (the paper treats this as an uncertain parameter, not a constant).
4. **Adjust up — multi-epoch training.** Repeat passes over data stretch the effective stock, but with diminishing returns; the paper caps the multiplier. Multiply by the epoch factor.
5. **Propagate uncertainty.** Run the whole ledger thousands of times, sampling each uncertain parameter from its range — that is the Monte Carlo step. The output is a window, not a date: 2026–2032, median 2028, at roughly 4e14 tokens of dataset size and ~5e28 FLOP of training compute for non-overtrained models (one to two years earlier if frontier models are overtrained).
6. **Now the agent-capacity computation.** Define E: HBM memory shipped 2025–27, expressed in GB300 equivalents. Define c: concurrent agent sessions one GB300 equivalent can serve — for closed models, infer it from API spending per agent-hour in TraceLab coding-agent traces (pooled rates Epoch reports: roughly $18/hour for GPT-5.5 on Codex and $15.5 for GPT-5.6 Sol, versus $24.3 for Opus 4.8 and $50.2 for Fable 5 on Claude Code; the report's reference point is $30/agent-hour); for open models, read it directly from AgentX serving benchmarks at a fixed 50 tokens/second streaming target.
7. **Multiply: A = E × c.** Epoch's headline (2026-10-02): roughly 30–170 million concurrent frontier-model agents — or about 1.9 billion concurrent sessions of an efficient open model (DeepSeek V4 Pro serving benchmarks).
8. **The demand check — the step most forecasters skip.** Convert capacity to dollars. Using only 20% of central capacity implies $2.6–5.3 trillion per year in API-equivalent spending, against roughly $1 trillion in combined developer revenue projected by end-2027 (at fivefold annual growth). If demand can't absorb the capacity, the binding constraint isn't chips — it's customers. That is the capacity-glut warning.
9. **Date your work.** Write 'as of 2026-10-07' on every figure. The 2022 data-wall estimate said ~2024; it was revised to ~2028 when web data filtered better than assumed. Your forecast is a perishable artifact — the method above is durable, the numbers are not.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Your capstone for this module: build your own bounded forecast with stated assumptions. Pick one frontier quantity — examples: the inference cost of a fixed benchmark capability in 2028, the data-stock exhaustion date under a different overtraining assumption, or the agent capacity of a single year's HBM shipments. Deliverable: a one-page forecast memo with (1) the quantity and why it matters, (2) an assumption table with a source or an explicit guess for each input, (3) a central estimate plus an uncertainty interval, (4) an as-of date and a decay plan — what would make you revise it. Grading bar: every number dated, every assumption stated, no point estimates without intervals. If your memo could be quoted in 2028 without embarrassing you, it isn't honest enough — put the uncertainty in writing.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: What decays here: model names and hourly rates (GPT-5.6 Sol, Opus 4.8, Fable 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro are Epoch's 2026 estimates and assumptions), HBM shipment figures, the ~47%/quarter cost-curve rate, and the 30–170M capacity range itself — all as-of 2026-10-02/07. What endures: the method — ledger both sides, adjust honestly, propagate uncertainty, report intervals, date everything. And the meta-lesson: the binding constraint moves. In 2022 the debate was training-data supply; by 2026 it is inference economics and demand. Any forecaster who reports a date without naming the constraint they're assuming is selling certainty they don't have.

cards.front: What is capability forecasting, in one sentence?
cards.back: Converting unobservable quantities about AI's future — usable data remaining, deployable agent capacity, cost of a fixed capability — into bounded forecasts with stated assumptions and uncertainty intervals.

cards.front: The data-wall model: both sides of the ledger?
cards.back: Demand: scaling laws tie dataset size to ~sqrt(training compute), so data demand compounds. Supply: indexed-web text estimated from Google's index size and Common Crawl bytes-per-page, converted to tokens.

cards.front: The two adjustments to raw web-token counts — and their directions?
cards.back: Quality filtering shrinks the effective stock (only a usable fraction trains well); multi-epoch training stretches it (repeat passes, capped multiplier).

cards.front: The data-wall headline forecast (window, median, scale)?
cards.back: 2026–2032 window, median 2028: datasets approaching ~4e14 tokens, ~5e28 FLOP of training compute for non-overtrained models — a year or two earlier if overtrained. (Villalobos et al., as of 2026-10-07.)

cards.front: Epoch's agent-capacity formula and its terms?
cards.back: A = E × c. E = effective hardware supply (HBM shipped 2025–27, in GB300 equivalents). c = concurrent agent sessions per GB300 — from TraceLab $/agent-hour traces (closed) or AgentX serving benchmarks (open).
~30–170M concurrent frontier-model agents from 2025–27 HBM shipments — or ~1.9B concurrent sessions of an efficient open model (DeepSeek V4 Pro benchmarks).

cards.front: Why does Epoch say demand, not chips, is the binding unknown?
cards.back: 20% of central capacity implies $2.6–5.3T/year in API-equivalent spending vs ~$1T projected developer revenue by end-2027 — a potential capacity glut.
Cost of a fixed level of benchmark performance falling ~47%/quarter (~13×/year) since 2023 — faster than electricity, compute, batteries, or DNA sequencing ever fell. (Epoch, Sep 2026.)

cards.front: The decay lesson in one line?
cards.back: The 2022 data-wall estimate said ~2024; it was revised to ~2028 when web data filtered better than assumed. Every frontier number is a dated artifact.

cards.front: Chip-supply tracking: what does Epoch's corpus monitor?
cards.back: AI data centers worldwide (satellite imagery, H100-equivalents, capex), chip-shock exposure (China ~2.7× the US), and trade-data anomalies like ~$3B of chips routed via Malaysia.

cards.front: Adoption measurement: two signals Epoch tracks?
cards.back: Coding-agent usage doubling roughly monthly; AI-use acknowledgments in arXiv math preprints rising 4%→25% (Apr→Aug 2026).
When buildout outruns demand: the hardware can serve far more agents than customers will pay for — Epoch's warning for the 2025–27 HBM buildout.

cards.front: As-of discipline: what three things must a frontier forecast carry?
cards.back: Stated assumptions, an uncertainty interval (not a point estimate), and an as-of date with a decay plan.

modules.title: Measuring AI Itself: RE-Bench and the Task-Time Horizon
modules.summary: Welcome to the module where AI gets measured. I'm your instructor, and our subject is METR — the independent evaluation nonprofit whose benchmarks are the field's most cited answer to the question 'how capable are these systems, really?' You'll study RE-Bench, where AI agents and human experts compete head-to-head at real machine-learning research engineering, and the time-horizon method, which compresses 'how autonomous is this model?' into a single fitted number. You'll also learn what the numbers don't say — because reading an evaluation means reading its fine print. All fast-moving figures: as of October 7, 2026.
objectives: Describe RE-Bench's design and motivation: contamination-free environments built to measure AI automation of AI R&D — a capability of concern — with calibrated scoring and faithful human baselines
Explain the crossover finding: agents win at 2-hour budgets, humans at 8-hour and 32-hour budgets, and why
Define the time-horizon metric and how it is fitted from human task times and model success curves
Report the ~7-month doubling trend (2019-2025) and the TH1.1 update's faster post-2023 estimate (130.8 days)

Identify the limits of both instruments — RE-Bench's seven environments and fast feedback loops, time horizons as suite-specific fitted estimates — and apply a critical checklist to any capability evaluation: comparison fairness, contamination, baselining quality, and suite-sensitivity

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **RE-Bench** — METR's benchmark (announced 2024-11-22) for AI-led ML research engineering: seven realistic, open-ended environments where agents and human experts compete with the same resources and time limits.
- **Anti-contamination design** — RE-Bench environments are built from scratch so they cannot appear in models' training data; most environments are held back unpublished for the same reason.
- **Calibrated scoring** — Each environment's score is normalized so 0 = the starting solution's score and 1 = METR's strong reference solution.
- **Human baselines** — 71 paid attempts by 61 distinct human experts, each given up to 8 hours; 82% reached a non-zero score, 24% matched or beat the reference.
- **The 2h/8h/32h crossover** — Best agents score ~4× humans at a 2-hour budget; humans narrowly lead at 8 hours and reach ~2× the top agent score at 32 hours (across attempts).
- **Time horizon (P50/P80)** — METR's autonomy metric: the human-expert task length at which an agent has a 50% (or 80%) chance of success, read off a fitted curve.
- **Logistic fit** — The fitting method: plot model success probability against human task length, fit a logistic curve, read the length where it crosses 50%.
- **Doubling time (195.8 days)** — The 50%-reliability horizon doubles roughly every 7 months (2019–2025); 95% CI [162, 223] days.
- **Time Horizon 1.1** — METR's January 2026 refresh: 170→228 tasks, long tasks doubled 14→31, infrastructure moved from Vivaria to Inspect; post-2023 doubling 130.8 days (95% CI [107, 161]).
- **Capability of concern** — Frontier safety policies single out automation of AI R&D by AI agents; RE-Bench is built as the reusable instrument for monitoring exactly that.
- **Suite sensitivity** — Time horizons are fitted, suite-specific estimates — change the task mix and the number moves. Not a claim about automating jobs.
- **Saturation** — Fully saturating RE-Bench would mean agents significantly outperforming top ML engineers in this setting; the benchmark's small size is deliberate.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
In this section you'll do what an evaluator does: read a horizon curve and score a research-engineering task. No code needed — a pencil works.
1. **Assemble the suite.** Collect a diverse set of multi-step software/research tasks and time human experts on each — you need real human-minutes per task, not vibes.
2. **Run the model.** Record success/failure on each task at a fixed attempt budget.
3. **Fit the curve.** Plot success probability against human task length and fit a logistic curve. The P50 time horizon is the task length where the fitted curve crosses 50% success. (Current frontier: near 100% success on sub-4-minute human tasks, under 10% past ~4 human-hours — measured 2025-03-19.)
4. **Track generations.** Repeat for successive models and fit the trend of P50 horizons over calendar time. METR's result: doubling every 195.8 days (~7 months), 95% CI [162, 223].
5. **Stress-test the trend.** METR's sensitivity analysis: even a 10× error in absolute measurement shifts the arrival of 'month-long tasks' by only ~2 years. That's what a robust trend looks like.
6. **Apply the TH1.1 update.** With 228 tasks and the Inspect infrastructure, the long-run doubling stays ~7 months (196.5 days), but post-2023 it's 130.8 days — 20% faster. Note the caveat METR states: part genuine acceleration, part suite composition change.
7. **Now score an RE-Bench-style task.** Setup: give the solver (human or agent) a computer with GPUs, a scoring function (maximize accuracy, minimize runtime), and a fixed time budget. Normalize: 0 = starting score, 1 = reference solution. Example (from METR's report): prefix-sum GPU kernel — starting code 4.74 ms, reference solution 1.60 ms, best human expert 0.67 ms, o1-preview's custom CUDA kernel 0.64 ms. Score each attempt; compare best-of-k across budgets: agents dominate at 2h, humans at 8h and 32h.
8. **Read the fine print before citing.** Only 7 environments; faster feedback loops than real research; measurements above ~16 human-hours are unreliable with the current suite.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Design a contamination-free evaluation for a capability claim. Pick a claim you have actually seen (e.g., 'our agent completes 8-hour software tasks autonomously'). Deliverable: a 2-page eval design with (1) 3+ environments built from scratch, with scoring functions and calibrated 0–1 scales; (2) a human-baselining plan (who, how many attempts, what time budget); (3) an anti-contamination plan (what's published, what's held back); (4) the metric you'll report and how you'll fit it; (5) a limitations section naming at least three ways your eval could mislead. Grading bar: if your limitations section is shorter than your results section, rewrite it.

notes.title: Frontier honesty
notes.body: What decays: horizon values, doubling estimates (TH1 vs TH1.1 already differ), model scores on RE-Bench — all as-of 2026-10-07. What the metric does not claim: that models 'work 16 hours' in any ordinary sense, that whole jobs are automated, or that the trend extrapolates past the suite's reliable range. What endures: the method — contamination-free environments, calibrated human baselines, fitted success curves, stated confidence intervals. And METR's own caution, which we adopt as policy: the time horizon is a suite-specific fitted estimate of autonomous task-completion capability. Quote the interval, not the point.

scriptLabs.title: Hype-pattern audit: dissect a frontier claim
scriptLabs.brief: Take a real frontier claim (a press release, a paper abstract, or a social-media post) and run the module's hype-pattern audit: pin the exact assertion, date it, check the base rate, and render a dated verdict.
scriptLabs.starter:
# Hype-pattern audit: <claim, quoted>
# 1. CLAIM (the exact assertion, quoted — not the headline's version):
# 2. AS-OF (date of the claim; date of the underlying evidence):
# 3. BASE RATE (how often do claims of this type pan out?):
# 4. HYPE PATTERNS (which patterns from the module appear? stale baselines? metric gaming? category error?):
# 5. VERDICT (what survives, with a confidence and a review date):
scriptLabs.hint: Quote the exact assertion first — most hype dies at step 1, when the headline's claim turns out not to be the paper's claim. Then date everything before judging anything.
scriptLabs.solution:
# Hype-pattern audit: 'Quantum computer solves useful problem 10,000x faster' (headline, 2026-03)
# 1. CLAIM (paper): a 127-qubit device ran a materials-simulation subroutine with lower estimated runtime than the best-known classical method on that instance size.
# 2. AS-OF: claim 2026-03; evidence: single instance, contrived benchmark; no error-corrected logical qubits involved.
# 3. BASE RATE: 'quantum advantage' headlines precede retractions or qualifications roughly as often as not — strong prior against.
# 4. HYPE PATTERNS: headline inflation (paper is narrower than headline); single-instance result; no scaling argument.
# 5. VERDICT: genuine incremental progress on one benchmark; not evidence of useful quantum advantage. Confidence: moderate. Review: 2027-03.

scriptLabs.title: Fermi estimation: reproduce a scaling claim
scriptLabs.brief: Pick a frontier scaling claim (training-compute growth, sequencing-cost decline, launch-cost decline) and reproduce it as an order-of-magnitude Fermi estimate: state assumptions, compute, then sanity-check against a known anchor.
scriptLabs.starter:
# Fermi estimate: <claim>
# 1. ASSUMPTIONS (each with a source or a stated guess):
# 2. ESTIMATE (the arithmetic, showing orders of magnitude):
# 3. SANITY CHECK (anchor against a known quantity — does it land within 10x?):
# 4. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER (the two most load-bearing assumptions):
scriptLabs.hint: Round aggressively — powers of ten only. The point is the order of magnitude and which assumptions dominate, not the third significant figure.
scriptLabs.solution:
# Fermi estimate: 'training compute for frontier models grows ~4x per year'
# 1. ASSUMPTIONS: 2020 frontier ~1e23 FLOP (GPT-3 class, public estimates); 2024 frontier ~1e26 FLOP (public estimates); chip efficiency ~1.3x/yr; spend growth fills the rest.
# 2. ESTIMATE: 1e26/1e23 = 1e3 over 4 years → ~5.6x/yr raw; net of efficiency, ~4x/yr of effective compute. Order of magnitude: thousands-fold per half-decade.
# 3. SANITY CHECK: matches Epoch AI's published training-compute trend within a factor of a few — the estimate lands.
# 4. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER: (a) undisclosed training runs (could shift the anchor); (b) algorithmic efficiency gains (could decouple FLOP from capability).
